newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK--Greenspan at the pulpit.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK--Greenspan at the pulpit.

text.p: When Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan steps up to the pulpit next week to testify before Congress, U.S. credit market players will be all ears for subtle clues on monetary policy, analysts said.
Congress will hold its semi-annual monetary policy gathering, known as the Humphrey-Hawkins hearings, on Tuesday and Wednesday.
The central bank chairman is scheduled to speak to the House on Tuesday at 1400 EDT/1800 GMT and to the Senate on Wednesday at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT.
So what is Greenspan likely to preach about?

Anthony Chan, chief economist at Banc One Investment Advisors Corp, said he expected Greenspan's speech to suggest there may be indications that the U.S. economy might grow at a stronger pace in the second half of the year.
"That in itself will give Greenspan the latitude to indicate that the end of the Fed tightening (cycle) in 1997 is somewhat of a premature call," said Chan.
Greenspan received a considerable dose of bipartisan criticism for boosting the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent in March.
But analysts said the stellar performance of financial markets since the last Fed tightening -- combined with the economy's low jobless rate and dormant inflation -- could now earn Greenspan praise.
Greenspan has done an "excellent job," said Chan. "It's very difficult to argue with success."

Among other Fed speakers, Federal Reserve Vice Chair Alice Rivlin, Fed Governor Laurence Meyer and New York Fed President William McDonough will testify at a House Banking Committee hearing on Wednesday.
On Friday, Minneapolis Federal Reserve President Gary Stern delivers a speech in Red Wing, Minn.
The Treasury will bring fresh supply to the bond markets, offering $15.5 billion in two-year notes and $11.5 billion in five-year notes, on Tuesday and Wednesday, respectively.
Dan Seto, senior economist with Nikko Securities Co International Inc, said the new supply may be quickly sold.

"The bond market has been driven by expectations about the (federal) budget," said Seto. "The reason that we are at 6.50 percent on the long bond has a lot to do with the expectations of diminishing supply," he said.

With some Republican leaders currently lobbying for a bill calling for the use of federal budget surpluses to pay down outstanding Treasury debt, investors are beginning to adopt a "buy it while you can" sentiment, added Seto.
The Treasury Department is slated to release its budget statement for June on Tuesday, at 1400 EDT/1800 GMT. Experts in a Reuters poll forecast, on average, a surplus of $47.3 billion.
On Friday, the Commerce Department is set to release durable goods for June. Wall Street experts are calling for a 1.4-percent increase in orders, up from May's 0.6-percent level.
Also, existing home sales for June are scheduled for release on Friday. A Reuters poll found sales slipped to 4.19 million from 4.24 million in May.
